claim: Channelrhodopsins (ChRs) are light-gated ion channels widely used to optically activate or silence selected electrogenic cells, such as individual brain neurons.
source: Channelrhodopsins (ChRs) are light-gated ion channels widely used to optically activate or silence selected electrogenic cells, such as individual brain neurons.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about channelrhodopsins and their optogenetic applications.

claim: MsACR1 from Mantoniella squamata showed high sensitivity to yellow-green light with λmax at 555 nm.
source: The Mantoniella squamata ACR (MsACR1) showed high sensitivity to yellow-green light (λmax at 555 nm) and was further engineered for optogenetic applications.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing the wavelength sensitivity of MsACR1.

claim: A single amino-acid substitution in MsACR1 shifted the photosensitivity 20 nm toward red light.
source: A single amino-acid substitution that mimicked red-light-sensitive rhodopsins like Chrimson shifted the photosensitivity 20 nm toward red light and accelerated photocurrent kinetics.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data on the spectral shift caused by the mutation.

claim: The single amino-acid substitution in MsACR1 accelerated photocurrent kinetics.
source: A single amino-acid substitution that mimicked red-light-sensitive rhodopsins like Chrimson shifted the photosensitivity 20 nm toward red light and accelerated photocurrent kinetics.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data on the kinetic changes caused by the mutation.

claim: The mutant was named raACR for 'red and accelerated ACR'.
source: Hence, it was named red and accelerated ACR, raACR.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the naming of the mutant.

claim: Both MsACR1 wild-type and raACR mutant are capable optical silencers at low light intensities in mouse neurons in vitro.
source: Both wild-type and mutant are capable optical silencers at low light intensities in mouse neurons in vitro and in vivo, while raACR offers a higher temporal resolution.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data from in vitro neuronal recordings.

claim: Both MsACR1 wild-type and raACR mutant are capable optical silencers at low light intensities in mouse neurons in vivo.
source: Both wild-type and mutant are capable optical silencers at low light intensities in mouse neurons in vitro and in vivo, while raACR offers a higher temporal resolution.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data from in vivo experiments.

claim: raACR offers a higher temporal resolution than wild-type MsACR1.
source: Both wild-type and mutant are capable optical silencers at low light intensities in mouse neurons in vitro and in vivo, while raACR offers a higher temporal resolution.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data comparing the temporal resolution of the two variants.

claim: Channelrhodopsins are light-activated ion channels.
source: Channelrhodopsins (ChRs) are light-activated ion channels (Nagel et al., 2003; Nagel et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational work on channelrhodopsins.

claim: Many channelrhodopsins are found in algae with flagella and eyespot.
source: Many of them are found in algae with flagella and eyespot (Rozenberg et al., 2020), where they are used for phototactic movement (Baidukova et al., 2022; Govorunova et al., 2004; Sineshchekov et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Channelrhodopsins in algae are used for phototactic movement.
source: Many of them are found in algae with flagella and eyespot (Rozenberg et al., 2020), where they are used for phototactic movement (Baidukova et al., 2022; Govorunova et al., 2004; Sineshchekov et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Cation-conducting ChRs (CCRs) are repurposed in optogenetics to trigger electrical activity in excitable tissue through optically evoked membrane depolarization.
source: In optogenetics, cation-conducting ChRs (CCRs) are repurposed to trigger electrical activity in excitable tissue through optically evoked membrane depolarization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about optogenetic applications of CCRs.

claim: Natural and engineered anion-conducting ChRs (ACRs) are predominantly used to hyperpolarize the membrane potential in neurons to shunt electrical activity.
source: To shunt electrical activity in neurons, natural and engineered anion-conducting ChRs (ACRs) are predominantly used to hyperpolarize the membrane potential in neurons (Emiliani et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Potassium-selective CCRs (KCRs) have been discovered in stramenopiles and other heterotrophic flagellates.
source: Most recently, potassium-selective CCRs (KCRs) have been discovered in stramenopiles and other heterotrophic flagellates, offering additional potential to silence electrogenic cells (Govorunova et al., 2022; Vierock et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent publications.

claim: KCRs offer additional potential to silence electrogenic cells.
source: Most recently, potassium-selective CCRs (KCRs) have been discovered in stramenopiles and other heterotrophic flagellates, offering additional potential to silence electrogenic cells (Govorunova et al., 2022; Vierock et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents an inference about the functional potential of KCRs.

claim: An activation wavelength (λmax) in the red spectral range allows penetration in deeper layers than blue light.
source: An activation wavelength (λmax) in the red spectral range allows penetration in deeper layers than blue light (Ash et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on light penetration in tissue.

claim: Optogenetic tools that are sensitive to red light are desirable.
source: Therefore, optogenetic tools that are sensitive to red light are desirable.
evidence: This is an inference based on the advantage of red light penetration.

claim: RubyACRs from the Labyrinthulea are the most redshifted ACRs reported.
source: Currently, RubyACRs from the Labyrinthulea are the most redshifted ACRs reported.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field at the time of writing.

claim: RubyACRs exhibit a substantial photocurrent inactivation at high light intensities.
source: However, they exhibit a substantial photocurrent inactivation and a slow photocurrent recovery at high light intensities (Govorunova et al., 2020) caused by the accumulation of long-lasting and non-conducting secondary photointermediates (Sineshchekov et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on RubyACRs.

claim: RubyACRs exhibit a slow photocurrent recovery at high light intensities.
source: However, they exhibit a substantial photocurrent inactivation and a slow photocurrent recovery at high light intensities (Govorunova et al., 2020) caused by the accumulation of long-lasting and non-conducting secondary photointermediates (Sineshchekov et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on RubyACRs.

claim: The photocurrent inactivation and slow recovery of RubyACRs is caused by the accumulation of long-lasting and non-conducting secondary photointermediates.
source: However, they exhibit a substantial photocurrent inactivation and a slow photocurrent recovery at high light intensities (Govorunova et al., 2020) caused by the accumulation of long-lasting and non-conducting secondary photointermediates (Sineshchekov et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research explaining the mechanism.

claim: MsACR1 is a member of the prasinophyte ACR family.
source: Among them, MsACR1, a member of the prasinophyte ACR family (Rozenberg et al., 2020), was the most activated with yellow-green light of 555 nm.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on ACR classification.

claim: MsACR1 was the most activated with yellow-green light of 555 nm among the screened panel of ChRs.
source: Among them, MsACR1, a member of the prasinophyte ACR family (Rozenberg et al., 2020), was the most activated with yellow-green light of 555 nm.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the screening.

claim: A single mutation in MsACR1 caused a further redshift of the action spectrum.
source: Introducing substitutions into the wild-type MsACR1 protein revealed a single mutation that caused a further redshift of the action spectrum and accelerated the photocurrent kinetics.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from mutagenesis studies.

claim: A single mutation in MsACR1 accelerated the photocurrent kinetics.
source: Introducing substitutions into the wild-type MsACR1 protein revealed a single mutation that caused a further redshift of the action spectrum and accelerated the photocurrent kinetics.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from mutagenesis studies.

claim: MsACR1 and raACR are well expressed in neurons.
source: The ACRs are well expressed and reliably suppress activity with nano-watt light intensities.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of expression in neurons.

claim: MsACR1 and raACR reliably suppress neuronal activity with nano-watt light intensities.
source: The ACRs are well expressed and reliably suppress activity with nano-watt light intensities.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from neuronal recordings.

claim: raACR offers suppression of action potentials at a higher temporal resolution than MsACR1.
source: Additionally, raACR offers suppression of action potentials at a higher temporal resolution than MsACR1.
evidence: This is based on experimental data comparing the temporal properties of the two variants.

claim: The expressed opsin candidates represent multiple ChR subfamilies.
source: The expressed opsin candidates represent multiple ChR subfamilies, some coming from previously unexplored clades
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of the identified ChRs.

claim: Some of the expressed opsin candidates come from previously unexplored clades.
source: The expressed opsin candidates represent multiple ChR subfamilies, some coming from previously unexplored clades
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis showing novel clades.

claim: GpACR1 is a protein from the heterotrophic cryptomonad Goniomonas pacifica.
source: GpACR1, a protein from the heterotrophic cryptomonad Goniomonas pacifica unrelated to cryptophyte ACRs and instead putatively related to labyrinthulean ACRs
evidence: This is based on the identification and phylogenetic analysis of GpACR1.

claim: GpACR1 is unrelated to cryptophyte ACRs.
source: GpACR1, a protein from the heterotrophic cryptomonad Goniomonas pacifica unrelated to cryptophyte ACRs and instead putatively related to labyrinthulean ACRs
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: GpACR1 is putatively related to labyrinthulean ACRs.
source: GpACR1, a protein from the heterotrophic cryptomonad Goniomonas pacifica unrelated to cryptophyte ACRs and instead putatively related to labyrinthulean ACRs
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and represents an inference about evolutionary relationships.

claim: S16-ACR1 was discovered in the single-amplified genome (SAG) of the uncultured MAST3 stramenopile S16.
source: S16-ACR1, which we discovered in the single-amplified genome (SAG) of the uncultured MAST3 stramenopile S16 (Wideman et al., 2020), representing its own deeply branching clade
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis and is supported by a citation.

claim: S16-ACR1 represents its own deeply branching clade.
source: S16-ACR1, which we discovered in the single-amplified genome (SAG) of the uncultured MAST3 stramenopile S16 (Wideman et al., 2020), representing its own deeply branching clade
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: TaraACR3 is a haptophyte ACR of metagenomic origin.
source: TaraACR3, a haptophyte ACR of metagenomic origin
evidence: This is based on the identification and taxonomic classification of TaraACR3.

claim: TaraACR1 and TaraACR2 are two related ChR sequences coming from giant viruses.
source: and TaraACR1 and TaraACR2, two related ChR sequences coming from giant viruses (see Supplementary Discussion) and forming a separate ChR subfamily
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and taxonomic classification.

claim: TaraACR1 and TaraACR2 form a separate ChR subfamily.
source: and TaraACR1 and TaraACR2, two related ChR sequences coming from giant viruses (see Supplementary Discussion) and forming a separate ChR subfamily
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: All tested ChR constructs showed bidirectional photocurrents upon illumination, typical for ChRs.
source: All constructs showed bidirectional photocurrents upon illumination, typical for ChRs.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: MsACR1 showed no or only little photocurrent reduction under continuous illumination.
source: However, while MsACR1, TaraACR1, and TaraACR2 showed no or only little photocurrent reduction under continuous illumination (photocurrent inactivation), TaraACR3, S16-ACR1, and GpACR1 showed considerable inactivation.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: TaraACR1 showed no or only little photocurrent reduction under continuous illumination.
source: However, while MsACR1, TaraACR1, and TaraACR2 showed no or only little photocurrent reduction under continuous illumination (photocurrent inactivation), TaraACR3, S16-ACR1, and GpACR1 showed considerable inactivation.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: TaraACR2 showed no or only little photocurrent reduction under continuous illumination.
source: However, while MsACR1, TaraACR1, and TaraACR2 showed no or only little photocurrent reduction under continuous illumination (photocurrent inactivation), TaraACR3, S16-ACR1, and GpACR1 showed considerable inactivation.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: TaraACR3 showed considerable photocurrent inactivation under continuous illumination.
source: However, while MsACR1, TaraACR1, and TaraACR2 showed no or only little photocurrent reduction under continuous illumination (photocurrent inactivation), TaraACR3, S16-ACR1, and GpACR1 showed considerable inactivation.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: S16-ACR1 showed considerable photocurrent inactivation under continuous illumination.
source: However, while MsACR1, TaraACR1, and TaraACR2 showed no or only little photocurrent reduction under continuous illumination (photocurrent inactivation), TaraACR3, S16-ACR1, and GpACR1 showed considerable inactivation.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: GpACR1 showed considerable photocurrent inactivation under continuous illumination.
source: However, while MsACR1, TaraACR1, and TaraACR2 showed no or only little photocurrent reduction under continuous illumination (photocurrent inactivation), TaraACR3, S16-ACR1, and GpACR1 showed considerable inactivation.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: S16-ACR1 photocurrents showed almost complete inactivation similar to the previously described MerMAIDs and some cryptophyte CCRs.
source: In particular, S16-ACR1 photocurrents showed almost complete inactivation similar to the previously described MerMAIDs and some cryptophyte CCRs (Oppermann et al., 2019; Sineshchekov et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings and comparison with cited literature.

claim: The inactivation effect of S16-ACR1 was more pronounced at positive holding potentials.
source: This effect was more pronounced at positive holding potentials.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings at different holding potentials.

claim: GpACR1 photocurrents elicited a secondary peak photocurrent upon light-off.
source: GpACR1 photocurrents, on the other hand, elicited a secondary peak photocurrent upon light-off (Figure 1D) indicative of photointermediate inactivation during illumination (Berndt et al., 2009; Krause et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1D and is interpreted based on cited literature.

claim: The secondary peak photocurrent upon light-off in GpACR1 is indicative of photointermediate inactivation during illumination.
source: GpACR1 photocurrents, on the other hand, elicited a secondary peak photocurrent upon light-off (Figure 1D) indicative of photointermediate inactivation during illumination (Berndt et al., 2009; Krause et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on cited literature about similar phenomena.

claim: Most of the tested ChRs showed a λmax between 470 and 510 nm.
source: Most of the tested ChRs showed a λmax between 470 and 510 nm, while MsACR1 exhibited a considerable redshifted λmax at 555 nm
evidence: This is based on action spectra measurements.

claim: MsACR1 exhibited a considerable redshifted λmax at 555 nm compared to most other tested ChRs.
source: Most of the tested ChRs showed a λmax between 470 and 510 nm, while MsACR1 exhibited a considerable redshifted λmax at 555 nm (Figure 1B, C, and Appendix 1—figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on action spectra measurements shown in the figures.

claim: At −60 mV holding potential, photocurrent amplitudes of up to 10 nA were elicited.
source: At −60 mV holding potential, photocurrent amplitudes of up to 10 nA were elicited (Figure 1E), decaying with an off-kinetic (τoff) between 3 ms (TaraACR2) and 400 ms (GpACR1) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Photocurrents decayed with an off-kinetic (τoff) between 3 ms (TaraACR2) and 400 ms (GpACR1).
source: At −60 mV holding potential, photocurrent amplitudes of up to 10 nA were elicited (Figure 1E), decaying with an off-kinetic (τoff) between 3 ms (TaraACR2) and 400 ms (GpACR1) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The operative light sensitivity was proportional to τoff.
source: The operative light sensitivity was proportional to τoff.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between kinetics and light sensitivity.

claim: TaraACR3, GpACR1, and MsACR1, with slow off-kinetics, had a high light sensitivity with half-maximal activation at 20–40 µW/mm2.
source: TaraACR3, GpACR1, and MsACR1, with slow off-kinetics, had a high light sensitivity with half-maximal activation at 20–40 µW/mm2.
evidence: This is based on light titration experiments.

claim: TaraACR2 and S16-ACR1 photocurrents did not saturate at light intensities up to 4 mW/mm2, demonstrating a low operative light sensitivity.
source: In contrast, TaraACR2 and S16-ACR1 photocurrents did not saturate at light intensities up to 4 mW/mm2, demonstrating a low operative light sensitivity (Appendix 1—figure 3B, C).
evidence: This is based on light titration experiments shown in the appendix figures.

claim: Only the replacement of external Cl−, but not external Na+, resulted in photocurrent changes and a substantial shift in the reversal potential close to the Nernst potential of Cl−.
source: Only the replacement of [Cl−]ex, but not [Na+]ex, resulted in photocurrent changes and a substantial shift in the reversal potential (Erev) close to the Nernst potential (ENernst) of Cl− (Appendix 1—figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is based on ion selectivity experiments shown in the appendix figures.

claim: All tested ChRs are ACRs (anion-conducting channelrhodopsins).
source: Therefore, all tested ChRs are ACRs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ion selectivity experiments.

claim: A redshift in rhodopsins can be achieved by either increasing the polarity close to the β-ionone ring of the retinal chromophore or reducing the polarity in the proximity of the retinal Schiff base (RSB).
source: Generally, a redshift can be achieved by either increasing the polarity close to the β-ionone ring of the retinal chromophore or reducing the polarity in the proximity of the retinal Schiff base (RSB).
evidence: This is established knowledge about rhodopsin spectral tuning.

claim: The exchange of the conserved Proline in the β-ionone ring region (HsBR-P186) generally causes strong blue-shifts.
source: The exchange of the conserved Proline in this region (HsBR-P186; see Appendix 1—figure 2 for an alignment) generally causes strong blue-shifts (Lu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The G186P mutation in MsACR1 blue-shifts the activity.
source: However, the converse G186P mutation in MsACR1 also blue-shifts the activity (Figure 2D), as do all other tested replacements (G186C, G186H, and G186T), with a substantial amplitude reduction in the case of G186H (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: All tested replacements at position 186 in MsACR1 (G186C, G186H, and G186T) blue-shift the activity.
source: However, the converse G186P mutation in MsACR1 also blue-shifts the activity (Figure 2D), as do all other tested replacements (G186C, G186H, and G186T), with a substantial amplitude reduction in the case of G186H (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The G186H mutation in MsACR1 causes a substantial amplitude reduction.
source: However, the converse G186P mutation in MsACR1 also blue-shifts the activity (Figure 2D), as do all other tested replacements (G186C, G186H, and G186T), with a substantial amplitude reduction in the case of G186H (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Most tested replacements close to the β-ionone ring in MsACR1 either did not affect λmax or resulted in hypsochromic shifts.
source: Other tested replacements close to the β-ionone ring either did not affect λmax or resulted in hypsochromic shifts, including mutations mirroring residues unique to the recently described RubyACRs: W142Y, W182Q, and G186I (Figure 2D, Govorunova et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Mutations mirroring residues unique to RubyACRs (W142Y, W182Q, and G186I) in MsACR1 either did not affect λmax or resulted in hypsochromic shifts.
source: Other tested replacements close to the β-ionone ring either did not affect λmax or resulted in hypsochromic shifts, including mutations mirroring residues unique to the recently described RubyACRs: W142Y, W182Q, and G186I (Figure 2D, Govorunova et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 2D and comparison with cited literature.

claim: The F138N mutation in MsACR1 showed a small redshift.
source: The only exception was F138N, which showed a small redshift (Figure 2D) but also strongly increased τoff (Figure 2F and Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The F138N mutation in MsACR1 strongly increased τoff.
source: The only exception was F138N, which showed a small redshift (Figure 2D) but also strongly increased τoff (Figure 2F and Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 2F and Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: The F185Y mutation in MsACR1 resulted in a blue-shifted λmax.
source: Replacing F185, a residue oriented toward the putative counterion D215 (Figure 2A), with a Tyrosine (F185Y) also resulted in a blue-shifted λmax (Figure 2D) and increased τoff (Figure 2F and Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The F185Y mutation in MsACR1 increased τoff.
source: Replacing F185, a residue oriented toward the putative counterion D215 (Figure 2A), with a Tyrosine (F185Y) also resulted in a blue-shifted λmax (Figure 2D) and increased τoff (Figure 2F and Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 2F and Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: The T87A mutation in MsACR1 led to a minor redshift.
source: Substitution of T87 with Alanine led to a minor redshift (Figure 2D) but decreased photocurrent amplitudes and decelerated τoff (Figure 2E, F and Appendix 1—figure 4, Oda et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The T87A mutation in MsACR1 decreased photocurrent amplitudes.
source: Substitution of T87 with Alanine led to a minor redshift (Figure 2D) but decreased photocurrent amplitudes and decelerated τoff (Figure 2E, F and Appendix 1—figure 4, Oda et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The T87A mutation in MsACR1 decelerated τoff.
source: Substitution of T87 with Alanine led to a minor redshift (Figure 2D) but decreased photocurrent amplitudes and decelerated τoff (Figure 2E, F and Appendix 1—figure 4, Oda et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 2F and Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: The T87V and T87S mutations in MsACR1 did not affect the spectral sensitivity.
source: Introduction of Valine or Serine (T87V and T87S) did not affect the spectral sensitivity (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In Chrimson, the residue A298 next to the retinal-binding Lysine was associated with the redshifted absorption of this ChR.
source: Previously, in Chrimson, the residue A298 next to the retinal-binding Lysine was associated with the redshifted absorption of this ChR (Oda et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: In MsACR1, the homologous residue to Chrimson A298 is S218.
source: In MsACR1, the homologous residue is S218.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment.

claim: The S218A mutation in MsACR1 reduced τoff fivefold.
source: Replacing it with an Alanine (MsACR1-S218A) reduced τoff fivefold (Figure 2F and Appendix 1—figure 4) and shifted λmax 20 nm toward longer wavelengths (Figure 2D and Appendix 1—figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 2F and Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: The S218A mutation in MsACR1 shifted λmax 20 nm toward longer wavelengths.
source: Replacing it with an Alanine (MsACR1-S218A) reduced τoff fivefold (Figure 2F and Appendix 1—figure 4) and shifted λmax 20 nm toward longer wavelengths (Figure 2D and Appendix 1—figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 2D and Appendix 1—figure 5A.

claim: The S218A mutation in MsACR1 shifted the half-maximal activity on the red side of the spectrum from 605 to 635 nm.
source: Consequently, the half-maximal activity on the red side of the spectrum also shifted from 605 to 635 nm (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on action spectra measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The S218A mutation in MsACR1 increased the photocurrent amplitude at 690 nm twofold in comparison with the wild-type.
source: Additionally, this mutation increased the photocurrent amplitude at 690 nm twofold in comparison with the wild-type.
evidence: This is based on photocurrent measurements at 690 nm.

claim: Relative to GtACR1, MsACR1-S218A exhibits a 19-fold larger photocurrent at 690 nm.
source: Relative to GtACR1, the most commonly used ACR for optogenetic application (Mahn et al., 2016; Tsunoda et al., 2017), MsACR1-S218A exhibits a 19-fold larger photocurrent at 690 nm (Appendix 1—figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on comparative photocurrent measurements shown in Appendix 1—figure 5C.

claim: GtACR1 is the most commonly used ACR for optogenetic application.
source: Relative to GtACR1, the most commonly used ACR for optogenetic application (Mahn et al., 2016; Tsunoda et al., 2017), MsACR1-S218A exhibits a 19-fold larger photocurrent at 690 nm (Appendix 1—figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Dissociated hippocampal neurons were transduced with adeno-associated viruses carrying the ACRs under the control of a pan-neuronal human Synapsin I (hSyn1) promoter.
source: We then transduced dissociated hippocampal neurons with adeno-associated viruses carrying the ACRs under the control of a pan-neuronal human Synapsin I (hSyn1) promoter.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: After 10 days, membrane-localized fluorescence was visible in somatic, axonal, and dendritic compartments without apparent intracellular or vesicular aggregation.
source: After 10 days, membrane-localized fluorescence was visible in somatic, axonal, and dendritic compartments without apparent intracellular or vesicular aggregation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on confocal imaging shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Current-evoked spiking was strongly suppressed in single neurons by 550 nm light at intensities of >200 nW/mm2.
source: Current-evoked spiking was strongly suppressed in single neurons by 550 nm light at intensities of >200 nW/mm2.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings in neurons.

claim: Excitation of MsACR1 at just 5 nW/mm2 light already decreased the spiking probability by 25%.
source: Excitation of MsACR1 at just 5 nW/mm2 light already decreased the spiking probability by 25%.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings in neurons.

claim: At light intensities between 100 and 7100 nW/mm2, evoked activity was reduced to 30–90% for both MsACR1 and raACR.
source: At light intensities between 100 and 7100 nW/mm2, evoked activity was further reduced to 30–90% for both ACRs (Figure 3B, C and Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3B, C and Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: MsACR1 and raACR both completely silenced current-evoked spiking during continuous illumination.
source: MsACR1 and raACR both completely silenced current-evoked spiking during continuous illumination (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3E.

claim: At the on-set of the light pulse, a light-evoked on-set spike was observed.
source: However, at the on-set of the light pulse, we observed a light-evoked on-set spike (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The on-set spike arises in axonal compartments with a higher intracellular chloride concentration compared to the soma, triggering initial chloride efflux upon ACR activation that leads to a short depolarization.
source: This has been similarly described for other ACRs and arises in axonal compartments with a higher intracellular chloride concentration compared to the soma, triggering initial chloride efflux upon ACR activation that leads to a short depolarization (Mahn et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an explanation based on cited literature about similar phenomena in other ACRs.

claim: Soma-targeted versions of MsACR1 and raACR were designed and tested to avoid misinterpretations arising from an on-set spike during in vivo optogenetic experiments.
source: To avoid misinterpretations arising from an on-set spike during in vivo optogenetic experiments, we designed and tested soma-targeted (st) versions of MsACR1 and raACR.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken.

claim: A short targeting sequence from the voltage-gated potassium channel Kv2.1 was fused to the N-terminus of the ACRs for soma targeting.
source: For this, we fused a short targeting sequence from the voltage-gated potassium channel Kv2.1 to the N-terminus of the ACRs.
evidence: This describes the molecular engineering approach.

claim: Pulsed illumination significantly reduced the on-set spike probability for both st-MsACR1 and st-raACR.
source: The latter significantly reduced the on-set spike probability for both variants (Appendix 1—figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Appendix 1—figure 7C.

claim: Compared to their untargeted versions, st-raACR showed a significantly reduced on-set spike probability.
source: Furthermore, compared to their untargeted versions, st-raACR showed a significantly reduced on-set spike probability, while st-MsACR1 showed a trend of a reduced on-set spike probability (Appendix 1—figure 7D).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Appendix 1—figure 7D.

claim: st-MsACR1 showed a trend of a reduced on-set spike probability compared to untargeted MsACR1.
source: Furthermore, compared to their untargeted versions, st-raACR showed a significantly reduced on-set spike probability, while st-MsACR1 showed a trend of a reduced on-set spike probability (Appendix 1—figure 7D).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Appendix 1—figure 7D.

claim: MsACR1 and st-MsACR1 nearly completely shunt all spikes during pulsed illumination independent of the light color.
source: MsACR1 and st-MsACR1 also nearly completely shunt all spikes during pulsed illumination independent of the light color.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Activation of raACR, or its soma-targeted version, significantly reduced the number of spikes under all conditions but with a lower potency compared to MsACR1.
source: Activation of raACR, or its soma-targeted version, significantly reduced the number of spikes under all conditions but with a lower potency compared to MsACR1 (Figure 3E and Appendix 1—figure 7B), likely due to the reduced ion flux during a single photocycle.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3E and Appendix 1—figure 7B.

claim: The lower potency of raACR compared to MsACR1 is likely due to the reduced ion flux during a single photocycle.
source: Activation of raACR, or its soma-targeted version, significantly reduced the number of spikes under all conditions but with a lower potency compared to MsACR1 (Figure 3E and Appendix 1—figure 7B), likely due to the reduced ion flux during a single photocycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic properties of raACR.

claim: raACR allows spike triggering with a 50% spiking frequency already 50 ms after optical silencing.
source: raACR allows spike triggering with a 50% spiking frequency already 50 ms after optical silencing, whereas upon activation of MsACR1, a 50% spiking frequency was reached only 180 ms post-shunting (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Upon activation of MsACR1, a 50% spiking frequency was reached only 180 ms post-shunting.
source: raACR allows spike triggering with a 50% spiking frequency already 50 ms after optical silencing, whereas upon activation of MsACR1, a 50% spiking frequency was reached only 180 ms post-shunting (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3G.

claim: A Monte Carlo simulation was used to model the brain tissue volume that could be effectively silenced.
source: We used a Monte Carlo simulation and our in vitro light titration data (Stujenske et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the computational modeling approach used.

claim: The comparison with other commonly used optogenetic attenuators (Jaws and GtACR1) showed the superiority of MsACR1 and raACR.
source: The comparison with other commonly used optogenetic attenuators (Jaws [Chuong et al., 2014] and GtACR1 [Govorunova et al., 2015]) showed the superiority of MsACR1 and raACR (Appendix 1—figure 8A, B).
evidence: This is based on Monte Carlo simulations shown in Appendix 1—figure 8A, B.

claim: High-titer viral particles of the ACRs were injected into the M1 of wild-type C57BL/6 mice.
source: As such, we injected high-titer viral particles of the ACRs into the M1 of wild-type C57BL/6 mice and implanted a 200-µm optical fiber above the injection site (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes the in vivo experimental procedure.

claim: A 200-µm optical fiber was implanted above the injection site in the M1.
source: As such, we injected high-titer viral particles of the ACRs into the M1 of wild-type C57BL/6 mice and implanted a 200-µm optical fiber above the injection site (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes the in vivo experimental procedure.

claim: Both MsACR1 and raACR exhibit homogenous expression in cortical neurons without visible intracellular aggregates or cell death.
source: Both ACRs exhibit homogenous expression in cortical neurons without visible intracellular aggregates or cell death (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Two-second illumination bouts with 635 nm light pulsed at 20 Hz led to immediate locomotion arrest in all tested animals.
source: Two-second illumination bouts with 635 nm light pulsed at 20 Hz led to immediate locomotion arrest in all tested animals (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is based on behavioral experiments shown in Figure 4B, C.

claim: Activation of either MsACR1 or raACR led to significantly reduced velocity in mice.
source: Activation of either ACR led to significantly reduced velocity.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of locomotion behavior.

claim: The effect on velocity was more substantial for MsACR1 than raACR, likely due to its longer-lasting response.
source: However, the effect was more substantial for MsACR1, likely due to its longer-lasting response compared to raACR (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data and is interpreted based on the kinetic properties shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Expression was targeted exclusively to parvalbumin-positive inhibitory neurons (PV-Cre) utilizing soma-targeted versions of the ACRs.
source: As complete locomotion arrest upon light stimulation points to a complex disruption of M1 circuit function, we decided to dissect this complexity by targeting expression exclusively to parvalbumin-positive inhibitory neurons (PV-Cre) utilizing our soma-targeted versions.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach for cell-type-specific expression.

claim: A 32-channel single-wire optrode was implanted to measure neuronal network responses in vivo upon illumination directly.
source: Additionally, we implanted a 32-channel single-wire optrode to measure neuronal network responses in vivo upon illumination directly (Anikeeva et al., 2012; Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used for in vivo recordings.

claim: Complex changes in neuronal firing were observed, ranging from an immediate decrease or increase in neuronal spiking, delayed changes in firing rate during light stimulation, and resetting of the firing rate after stimulation.
source: As expected, we observed complex changes in neuronal firing, ranging from an immediate decrease or increase in neuronal spiking, delayed changes in firing rate during light stimulation, and resetting of the firing rate after stimulation (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on in vivo electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5B.

claim: During the first 100 ms within a blue light stimulation at 1 mW, 9 out of 33 units for MsACR1 showed at least a twofold change in standard deviation compared to baseline.
source: During the first 100 ms within a blue light stimulation at 1 mW, 9 out of 33 units for MsACR1 showed at least a twofold change in standard deviation (SD) compared to baseline (2 s before illumination), which increased to 16 units at 10 mW.
evidence: This is based on in vivo electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis.

claim: At 10 mW blue light, 16 out of 33 units for MsACR1 showed at least a twofold change in standard deviation compared to baseline.
source: During the first 100 ms within a blue light stimulation at 1 mW, 9 out of 33 units for MsACR1 showed at least a twofold change in standard deviation (SD) compared to baseline (2 s before illumination), which increased to 16 units at 10 mW.
evidence: This is based on in vivo electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis.

claim: For illumination with red light at either 1 or 10 mW, more than 75% of all units (51 units) responded with a change in firing rate for MsACR1.
source: For illumination with red light at either 1 or 10 mW, more than 75% of all units (51 units) responded with a change in firing rate.
evidence: This is based on in vivo electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis.

claim: The fast-cycling raACR shows a superior inhibition at blue and red illumination regimes at 10 mW compared to MsACR1, exhibiting a modulation of neuronal spiking in more than 90% of units.
source: Interestingly, the fast-cycling raACR shows a superior inhibition at blue and red illumination regimes at 10 mW compared to MsACR1, exhibiting a modulation of neuronal spiking in more than 90% of units.
evidence: This is based on in vivo electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis.

claim: At light intensities of 1 mW for both wavelengths, raACR showed moderate effects on the cortical activity of 35%.
source: At light intensities of 1 mW for both wavelengths, raACR showed moderate effects on the cortical activity of 35%.
evidence: This is based on in vivo electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis.

claim: For both MsACR1 and raACR, red light illumination leads to a significant decrease in running speed at 10 mW light intensities.
source: In both cases, for MsACR1 and raACR, red light illumination leads to a significant decrease in running speed at 10 mW light intensities.
evidence: This is based on behavioral analysis during in vivo experiments.

claim: Control animals injected with hSyn1-DIO-eGFP do not show a significant change in running speed upon illumination.
source: Control animals injected with hSyn1-DIO-eGFP do not show a significant change (Mann–Whitney U, p > 0.05 control, p < 0.001 for MsACR1 and raACR) (Appendix 1—figure 9A, B).
evidence: This is based on behavioral analysis of control animals shown in Appendix 1—figure 9A, B.

claim: Despite the rapidly evolving optogenetic toolbox, highly efficient red-light-activatable tools are still sparse.
source: Despite the rapidly evolving optogenetic toolbox that offers versatile possibilities to manipulate the electrical activity of excitable cells, highly efficient red-light-activatable tools are still sparse.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field.

claim: The wild-type MsACR1 may offer a venue for answering questions about algal phototaxis.
source: Besides its availability as a useful optogenetic tool, the wild-type MsACR1 may also offer a venue for answering questions about algal phototaxis.
evidence: This is speculation about potential research applications.

claim: In motile prasinophytes, both ACRs and CCRs may cooperate to regulate photo-orientation.
source: Previously, we suggested that in motile prasinophytes, both ACRs and CCRs may cooperate to regulate photo-orientation (Rozenberg et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Proton conduction has been shown for CCR1 from M. squamata.
source: Recently, proton conduction has been shown for CCR1 from M. squamata (Govorunova et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: M. squamata may be a suitable algae species to investigate the physiological function of proton- and chloride-carried photocurrents.
source: Therefore, M. squamata may be a suitable algae species to investigate the physiological function of proton- and chloride-carried photocurrents.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of both types of channelrhodopsins in M. squamata.

claim: TaraACR1 and TaraACR2 are of viral origin.
source: Furthermore, among the characterized ACRs are two of viral origin, TaraACR1 and TaraACR2.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and taxonomic classification.

claim: These viral rhodopsins constitute a further contribution to the growing number of rhodopsins from viruses.
source: These proteins constitute a further contribution to the growing number of rhodopsins from viruses (Yutin and Koonin, 2012; Bratanov et al., 2019; Needham et al., 2019; Rozenberg et al., 2020; Zabelskii et al., 2020; Hososhima et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on viral rhodopsins.

claim: Compared to some of the previously characterized viral rhodopsin channels, TaraACR1 and TaraACR2 were well expressed and showed large photocurrents.
source: Compared to some of the previously characterized viral rhodopsin channels (Rozenberg et al., 2020; Zabelskii et al., 2020), the two described here were well expressed and showed large photocurrents.
evidence: This is based on experimental data and comparison with cited literature.

claim: TaraACR2 showed fast photocurrent off-kinetics comparable to ZipACR and RapACR.
source: Also, TaraACR2 showed fast photocurrent off-kinetics comparable to ZipACR and RapACR (Govorunova et al., 2018; Govorunova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on experimental data and comparison with cited literature.

claim: GpACR1 and S16-ACR1 are unsuitable for optogenetic applications due to their photocurrent amplitudes and kinetics.
source: While GpACR1 and S16-ACR1 are unsuitable for optogenetic applications due to their photocurrent amplitudes and kinetics, their photocurrents unravel interesting molecular features.
evidence: This is an assessment based on the experimental characterization of these proteins.

claim: GpACR1 photocurrents elicit a second peak upon light shut-off, a behavior seen before for the slow-cycling CrChR2 variant C128S, ReaChR, or the viral rhodopsin VirChR1.
source: GpACR1 photocurrents elicit a second peak upon light shut-off, a behavior seen before for the slow-cycling CrChR2 variant C128S (Berndt et al., 2009), ReaChR (Krause et al., 2017), or the viral rhodopsin VirChR1 (Zabelskii et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on experimental data and comparison with cited literature.

claim: The appearance of a second peak upon light shut-off is expected to be caused by the back photoisomerization of photocycle intermediates.
source: Its appearance is expected to be caused by the back photoisomerization of photocycle intermediates (Krause et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on cited literature.

claim: S16-ACR1 shows a substantial voltage-dependent photocurrent inactivation and nearly complete inward rectification similar to MerMAIDs.
source: S16-ACR1, on the other hand, shows a substantial voltage-dependent photocurrent inactivation and nearly complete inward rectification similar to MerMAIDs (Oppermann et al., 2019) and may offer further insight into these processes in general.
evidence: This is based on experimental data and comparison with cited literature.

claim: S16-ACR1 may offer further insight into voltage-dependent photocurrent inactivation and inward rectification processes in general.
source: S16-ACR1, on the other hand, shows a substantial voltage-dependent photocurrent inactivation and nearly complete inward rectification similar to MerMAIDs (Oppermann et al., 2019) and may offer further insight into these processes in general.
evidence: This is speculation about potential research applications.

claim: The action spectrum of MsACR1 shows its highest activity in yellow-green light and a distinct blue-light peak.
source: The action spectrum of MsACR1 shows its highest activity in yellow-green light and a distinct blue-light peak, probably resembling the β-band absorption of the retinal chromophore originating from two-photon absorption (Stavenga et al., 1993).
evidence: This is based on action spectra measurements.

claim: The distinct blue-light peak in MsACR1's action spectrum probably resembles the β-band absorption of the retinal chromophore originating from two-photon absorption.
source: The action spectrum of MsACR1 shows its highest activity in yellow-green light and a distinct blue-light peak, probably resembling the β-band absorption of the retinal chromophore originating from two-photon absorption (Stavenga et al., 1993).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on cited literature about retinal chromophore absorption.

claim: Most of the substitutions in MsACR1 close to the β-ionone ring resulted in a blue-shift.
source: Surprisingly, most of the substitutions in MsACR1 close to the β-ionone ring resulted in a blue-shift.
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments.

claim: Alternatively, the β-ionone ring could be twisted, which decouples it from the rest of the polyene chain.
source: Alternatively, the β-ionone ring could be twisted, which decouples it from the rest of the polyene chain (Kato et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation about the structural basis for the spectral properties, supported by a citation.

claim: The active site around the RSB was more susceptible to modification than the β-ionone ring region.
source: In contrast, the active site around the RSB was more susceptible to modification, although the effect of MsACR1-T87A was less pronounced than for Chrimson (ChrimsonSA) (Oda et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments and comparison with cited literature.

claim: The effect of MsACR1-T87A was less pronounced than for Chrimson (ChrimsonSA).
source: In contrast, the active site around the RSB was more susceptible to modification, although the effect of MsACR1-T87A was less pronounced than for Chrimson (ChrimsonSA) (Oda et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on comparison with cited literature.

claim: Replacing S218 with Alanine in MsACR1 mimics several orange- or red-light-absorbing ChRs.
source: However, upon replacing S218 with Alanine, the action spectrum was shifted by 20 nm toward longer wavelengths, mimicking several orange- or red-light-absorbing ChRs (Oda et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments and comparison with cited literature.

claim: Similar spectral shifts have been achieved naturally and artificially in animal rhodopsins.
source: Similar shifts have been achieved naturally and artificially in animal rhodopsins (Liénard et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Both MsACR1 and raACR reliably shunt spiking in vitro and induced motor arrest in vivo using 635 nm light.
source: Both MsACR1 and raACR reliably shunt spiking in vitro and induced motor arrest in vivo using 635 nm light.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from in vitro and in vivo experiments.

claim: Shunting during continuous illumination was complete for both MsACR1 and raACR.
source: Shunting during continuous illumination was complete, though light-evoked on-set spikes observed for both ACRs were minimized with pulsed illumination and soma targeting of MsACR1 and raACR.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Light-evoked on-set spikes observed for both ACRs were minimized with pulsed illumination and soma targeting.
source: Shunting during continuous illumination was complete, though light-evoked on-set spikes observed for both ACRs were minimized with pulsed illumination and soma targeting of MsACR1 and raACR.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Longer photon exposure is presumably required to evoke the on-set spike, as previously evident for GtACR1 using 10 ms light pulses.
source: Presumably, longer photon exposure is required to evoke this spike, as previously evident for GtACR1 using 10 ms light pulses (Mahn et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited literature about similar phenomena.

claim: Shorter or ramped-on light pulses can reduce the probability of on-set spike events.
source: Therefore, shorter or ramped-on light pulses can reduce the probability of such events.
evidence: This is an inference based on the understanding of the on-set spike mechanism.

claim: Pulsed illumination and soma targeting are recommended for artifact-free in vivo optogenetic experiments.
source: Overall, pulsed illumination and soma targeting are recommended for artifact-free in vivo optogenetic experiments.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Pulsed illumination was more efficient for MsACR1 due to its slower kinetics, resulting in increased ion flux per photocycle.
source: Pulsed illumination was more efficient for MsACR1. This was due to its slower kinetics, resulting in increased ion flux per photocycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic properties of MsACR1.

claim: The accelerated kinetics of raACR allows for a higher temporal resolution, enabling current-evoked spiking already 50 ms post-illumination.
source: On the other hand, the accelerated kinetics of raACR allows for a higher temporal resolution, enabling current-evoked spiking already 50 ms post-illumination.
evidence: This is based on experimental data on temporal resolution.

claim: Ideally, one would slow the kinetics of raACR to increase the efficiency under pulsed illumination.
source: Ideally, one would slow its kinetics to increase the efficiency of raACR under pulsed illumination.
evidence: This is speculation about potential improvements.

claim: Most mutations tested that resulted in slowed kinetics also shifted λmax to the blue.
source: However, most mutations tested here that resulted in slowed kinetics also shifted λmax to the blue.
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments.

claim: T87A or T87S could be potential candidates for combining with raACR, as they did not affect λmax but increased τoff while the current amplitudes were only marginally reduced.
source: Potential candidates for combining could be T87A or T87S, as they did not affect λmax but increased τoff while the current amplitudes were only marginally reduced.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future engineering strategies based on the mutagenesis data.

claim: Screening mutations of the homologous residues to the DC pair of CrChR2 could be fruitful for improving raACR.
source: On the other hand, screening mutations of the homologous residues to the DC pair of CrChR2 could be fruitful, as recently demonstrated (Rodriguez-Rozada et al., 2022).
evidence: This is speculation about potential future engineering strategies supported by a citation.

claim: In contrast to other ACRs commonly used as optogenetic silencers, both MsACR1 and raACR do not show substantial photocurrent inactivation during continuous illumination.
source: Also, in contrast to other ACRs commonly used as optogenetic silencers, both MsACR1 and raACR do not show substantial photocurrent inactivation during continuous illumination and can be activated again virtually instantly without photocurrent decline.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: MsACR1 and raACR can be activated again virtually instantly without photocurrent decline.
source: Also, in contrast to other ACRs commonly used as optogenetic silencers, both MsACR1 and raACR do not show substantial photocurrent inactivation during continuous illumination and can be activated again virtually instantly without photocurrent decline.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The lack of substantial photocurrent inactivation recommends MsACR1 and raACR as reliable optogenetic actuators.
source: This recommends them as reliable optogenetic actuators.
evidence: This is an inference based on the photocurrent properties.

claim: The redshifted raACR reduces potential cross-activation when used with blue-light-sensitive optogenetic actuators or reporter systems.
source: Furthermore, the redshifted raACR reduces potential cross-activation when used with blue-light-sensitive optogenetic actuators or reporter systems (Vierock et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference about the practical advantages of raACR, supported by a citation.

claim: MsACR1 and raACR, due to their good expression and membrane targeting, high chloride conductance and slow off kinetics provide a high operational light sensitivity to neuronal cells which enables inhibition at light intensities as low as 20 nW/mm2.
source: In conclusion, MsACR1 and raACR, due to their good expression and membrane targeting, high chloride conductance and slow off kinetics provide a high operational light sensitivity to neuronal cells which enables inhibition at light intensities as low as 20 nW/mm2.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Both MsACR1 and raACR are a valuable addition to the optogenetic toolbox when long-lasting inhibition in larger brain volumes is required.
source: Thus, we believe both ACRs are a valuable addition to the optogenetic toolbox when long-lasting inhibition in larger brain volumes is required.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental characterization and in vivo validation.
